title: Explanations are not what we say. They are what pupils understand.
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes attacks the assumption that explanation is a natural act that follows from subject knowledge, and recasts it as a design problem. Her worked example is a deliberately poor account of photosynthesis that is scientifically flawless and pedagogically useless because it loads vocabulary, a word equation, causal links and limiting factors on a learner who has not yet secured the basic idea. From a simple memory model - working memory is limited, attention is the gatekeeper, memory is the residue of thought - she derives a definition of explanation as engineering understanding rather than saying clear things. The expert blind spot explains why 'just listen carefully' is a poor answer to confusion: what the expert experiences as logical compression lands on the novice as a blur. Her constructive moves are to go from concrete experience to abstract idea, to lead with the question the explanation answers, and to use the 'zoom in, zoom out' discipline of moving between whole and part, illustrated in science and in teaching Macbeth. Situating explanation inside Rosenshine's sequence, she insists it is preparation rather than endpoint. The standard she sets is deliberately demanding: an explanation succeeds only when pupils can do something they previously could not, once the teacher has stopped talking.
points: The photosynthesis counter-example is the piece's best teaching tool: it shows that accuracy and clarity are not the same property, and that an explanation can be correct in every detail and still fail.

Hughes builds meaning from three ingredients - experience to attach the idea to, models to organise it, and situations that make it purposeful - which is why starting from a definition alone is weak teaching.
'Why first' is treated as orientation rather than motivation: pupils attend better when they know what question the explanation is answering.
The zoom in, zoom out move - big picture, specific detail, back out to the frame - is offered as what expert teachers often do unconsciously and should do deliberately.
Her closing test shifts the unit of judgement from teacher performance to pupil capability after the explanation ends.
quotes: One of the more damaging myths in teaching is the idea that explanation is somehow natural. You know your subject, you stand at the front, you tell pupils what they need to know, and if they do not get it, the problem is likely to be attention, effort, or perhaps motivation.

Everything in that explanation is scientifically accurate, but it comes as one long, unbroken stream. It introduces new vocabulary, a word equation, several causal links, and the idea of limiting factors all at once, before pupils have secured the basic idea that plants make their own food using light.
That gives us a more useful definition of explanation. It is not saying clear things. It is engineering understanding.

What experts experience as logical compression often lands on novices as a blur. The expert sees coherence because the gaps are filled by knowledge already stored in long-term memory. The novice sees fragments.

The point is that meaning is not simply transferred from teacher to pupil intact. Learners build understanding by connecting new ideas to something they can already perceive, imagine, or reason about.
Too often, teachers explain as if the act of saying it were the endpoint. It is not. The point of explanation is successful pupil thinking when the teacher is no longer talking.

When explanations fail, pupils are left with vague notes, shaky definitions and the uncomfortable sense that everyone else has understood something they have somehow missed. When explanations succeed, pupils can do something they could not previously do.
